title: What estate planning is: control, taxes, who decides when you cannot
summary: Estate planning decides three things in advance: who controls your affairs if you cannot, who receives what when you die, and how much tax and cost is lost along the way. It is a set of documents and structures that must agree with each other, not a single will.
body:
Bottom line. Estate planning is not only about death. It answers three questions in advance: who decides for you if you cannot, who receives your property when you die, and how much is lost to tax and cost. A will is one document in the plan. It is not the plan.

In plain English

Your estate is everything you own when you die, minus what you owe. Estate planning is arranging your affairs so that the right people make decisions and receive property, at the right time, with as little loss as the law allows.

There are two moments to plan for. The first is incapacity. Incapacity means you are alive but cannot make your own decisions, perhaps after an accident or an illness. The second is death. People plan for death and forget incapacity, yet incapacity can last for years, and a business still needs someone to sign cheques, deal with lenders and vote shares.

For a developer, the stakes are higher than usual. Projects have deadlines. Loans have covenants. Partners have rights under shareholder agreements. If nobody has authority to act for you, a project can stall while the family waits for a court to appoint someone.

The framework

Think of the plan as five parts that must fit together.

  1. Who decides about property if you cannot. An enduring power of attorney names a person to manage your money and property, and it continues if you lose capacity. The next lesson covers it.
  2. Who decides about your personal care if you cannot. A personal directive names a person to make health and personal decisions and can record your wishes.
  3. Who receives what at death. Your will names an executor, who is the person who manages your estate, and sets out gifts. Some assets do not pass under the will at all, such as many registered plans with a named beneficiary and land held in joint tenancy. A later lesson covers those traps.
  4. How the business continues. Your shareholder agreement, the company's articles and bylaws, and any key person insurance decide who controls the company after you. Key person insurance is insurance on someone's life owned by the business.
  5. Tax and cost. In Canada, death usually triggers tax on your property's growth. Probate, which is the court process confirming a will and the executor's authority, adds time and fees. Structures can soften both, as a later lesson explains as concepts.

The test of a plan is consistency. Each document must agree with the others. A will that leaves your company shares to two children equally does not help if the shareholder agreement forces a sale of those shares to your partner at death.

A worked example

This example is hypothetical. All numbers are round and invented for teaching.

A developer, aged 55, owns a holding company worth 3,000,000, a home worth 900,000 held jointly with his spouse, and an RRSP worth 400,000. He has a will from fifteen years ago and no power of attorney.

He suffers a stroke and cannot communicate for six months. His company has a 2,000,000 construction loan that needs a signed draw request each month. Nobody else is authorised to sign. The family must apply to court for someone to be appointed to manage his affairs, which takes time and money. Meanwhile the lender treats the missed draws as a problem and the project stops.

A plan would have prevented most of this: an enduring power of attorney naming his spouse with an adult child as backup, a second signing officer authorised in the company's own records, a personal directive, and a current will. The cost of those documents is small compared with one month of project delay.

Professional Sign-Off Required: wills and estates lawyer; corporate lawyer for company signing authority.

The beginner mistake

The beginner mistake is to believe a will is enough. A will does nothing while you are alive. It cannot let anyone sign for your company if you are in hospital.

The second mistake is to assume your spouse can automatically act for you. Being married does not, on its own, give a person legal authority over your property or your company [unverified — confirm independently].

How you will use it

Make an estate map on one page. Across the top, the five parts above. Down the side, your main assets: each company, each property, each registered account, each insurance policy. In each box, write who controls or receives it, and under which document. Empty boxes and conflicting boxes are your to-do list. Take the map to an estates lawyer and ask them to fix the gaps in one engagement, so the documents are drafted together and agree with each other.

Review the map after any major event: a new company, a large property, a marriage, a separation, a birth or a death in the family.
checklist: List your main assets: companies, properties, registered accounts, insurance.
Name who would manage your property and who would make personal decisions if you could not.
Check you have an enduring power of attorney and a personal directive.
Check your will is current and names an executor and a backup.
Note which assets pass outside the will, by beneficiary designation or joint ownership.
Confirm a second person can sign for each company.
Check that the will and the shareholder agreement agree.

selftest.q: A developer has a recent will but no power of attorney. He is in a coma for three months and his company must sign a loan renewal. Who can sign, and what should have been in place?
selftest.a: The will does not help while he is alive. Unless the company has another authorised signing officer, nobody can sign without a court appointment, which takes time. He should have had an enduring power of attorney, a personal directive, and a second signing officer authorised in the company's records. A wills and estates lawyer and a corporate lawyer should set these up together.

apply: Draw your one-page estate map with five columns and fill in what you know today.
sources: Concept lesson. No statute section, fee or rate is cited. The statement about a spouse's authority is tagged [unverified — confirm independently]. Figures hypothetical. Education only; not legal or tax advice.
signoff: Professional Sign-Off Required: wills and estates lawyer; corporate lawyer.

title: Powers of attorney and personal directives
summary: An enduring power of attorney lets a person you choose manage your money and property if you lose capacity, and a personal directive lets a person you choose make your health and personal decisions. Without them, your family may need a court order, and neither document automatically lets someone run your company.
body:
Bottom line. Two short documents decide who acts for you if you cannot. An enduring power of attorney covers money and property. A personal directive covers health and personal care. Neither, on its own, gives someone the power to act as director of your company, so plan that separately.

In plain English

A power of attorney is a document in which you, the donor, give another person, the attorney, the authority to deal with your money and property. "Attorney" here does not mean lawyer. It means the person you trust to act.

An ordinary power of attorney usually ends if you lose mental capacity, which is exactly when you need it most. An enduring power of attorney is written so that it continues, or starts, when you lose capacity. In Alberta, these are governed by the Powers of Attorney Act (Alberta), which sets formal requirements for signing [unverified — confirm independently].

A personal directive is the matching document for personal matters: health care, where you live, and similar decisions. It names an agent, the person who decides for you, and can record your wishes. In Alberta, this is governed by the Personal Directives Act (Alberta) [unverified — confirm independently].

If you have neither, your family may have to apply to court for an order appointing a trustee for property or a guardian for personal matters. In Alberta, that process is under the Adult Guardianship and Trusteeship Act (Alberta) [unverified — confirm independently]. It is slower, costs more, and the court, not you, chooses.

The framework

  1. Choose people, then backups. Pick one attorney and one agent, and an alternate for each. Consider whether two people should act together. Acting together adds a check but can slow decisions.
  2. Choose when it starts. An enduring power of attorney can start immediately, or spring into effect when a stated event happens, such as written confirmation of incapacity by a doctor. A springing document is safer but slower to use.
  3. Set the scope and limits. You can limit what the attorney may do: no gifts, no sale of certain land, or a duty to report to another family member.
  4. Meet the formal requirements. Signing rules, witnesses and, in some places, a lawyer's certificate of independent advice [unverified — confirm independently]. A document that fails these may be refused when it matters.
  5. Plan the business separately. An attorney can usually vote your shares as your property [unverified — confirm independently]. But being a director is a personal office, so an attorney generally cannot take your seat on the board [unverified — confirm independently]. Use the company's articles, bylaws or shareholder agreement to name an alternate signer, or a process for appointing a new director quickly.
  6. Tell people and store the originals. Your attorney, agent, bank and lawyer should know where the originals are.

A worked example

This example is hypothetical. All numbers are round and invented for teaching.

A developer is sole director and sole shareholder of a holding company with 1,500,000 of investments, and owns half of a project company with a partner. He signs an enduring power of attorney naming his spouse, with his adult daughter as alternate, and a personal directive naming his spouse as agent.

His lawyer adds two business steps. First, the holding company's shareholder can appoint a new director by resolution. Because his spouse, as attorney, can vote his shares, she can appoint a director quickly if he loses capacity [unverified — confirm independently]. Second, the project company's shareholder agreement is amended so that if either partner is incapacitated for 90 days, a named nominee may act on that partner's behalf.

Two years later he has a long illness. His spouse pays the household bills under the power of attorney, his daughter is appointed a director of the holding company, and the nominee keeps the project's approvals moving. No court application is needed.

Professional Sign-Off Required: wills and estates lawyer; corporate lawyer.

The beginner mistake

The beginner mistake is to sign a bank's own power of attorney form and think the job is done. It may cover only that bank. It may not be enduring. It does nothing for land, investments elsewhere or your company.

The second mistake is to choose an attorney for affection rather than ability. The attorney must keep records, keep your money separate from their own, and act in your interest. Pick someone who can do that, and who lives close enough to act.

How you will use it

Ask your lawyer for three documents in one meeting: an enduring power of attorney, a personal directive, and a short note on how each of your companies would get a signing director if you could not act. Then test the plan with one question: "If I were in hospital tomorrow, could the next loan draw be signed this week?" If the answer is no, the plan is not finished. Review the documents whenever a chosen person moves away, becomes ill, or your relationship changes.
checklist: Name an attorney for property and an agent for personal decisions, with alternates.
Decide whether the power of attorney starts now or on a stated event.
Set limits, such as no gifts and a duty to report.
Sign with the formal requirements your lawyer confirms for your province.
Arrange a way for each company to get a signing director if you cannot act.
Store originals and tell the people named where they are.
Review whenever a named person's situation changes.

selftest.q: You are the only director of your company. You sign an enduring power of attorney naming your brother. You then lose capacity. Can your brother sign company contracts as director?
selftest.a: Generally not. A power of attorney covers your property, which can include voting your shares, but being a director is a personal office the attorney usually cannot exercise. Your brother may be able to vote your shares to appoint a new director, depending on the company's documents and the law. The safer plan is to name an alternate signer or a process in the company's articles, bylaws or shareholder agreement. A wills and estates lawyer and a corporate lawyer must confirm.

apply: Write down who you would want as your attorney and your agent, and one alternate for each, and book a meeting to make it formal.
sources: Powers of Attorney Act (Alberta), Personal Directives Act (Alberta) and Adult Guardianship and Trusteeship Act (Alberta) are named; their formal requirements and effects are tagged [unverified — confirm independently]. The rules on an attorney voting shares and acting as director are tagged [unverified — confirm independently] and depend on the company's documents and the current law. Figures hypothetical. Education only; not legal advice.
signoff: Professional Sign-Off Required: wills and estates lawyer; corporate lawyer.

title: The deemed disposition at death and how structures soften it
summary: In Canada, a person is generally treated as selling all their capital property at fair market value immediately before death, so tax is due on the growth even though nothing was sold. A spousal rollover, an estate freeze, insurance and careful post-death planning can defer, cap or fund that tax.
body:
Bottom line. Canada has no estate tax by that name, but death usually triggers income tax on the growth in everything you own. The tax is due even though no cash came in. Planning can defer it to a spouse, cap it at today's value, or make sure there is cash to pay it.

In plain English

A capital gain is the increase in value of a property between when you got it and when you dispose of it. Normally you pay tax on a capital gain only when you sell.

Death changes that. Under section 70(5) of the Income Tax Act (Canada), a person is generally deemed, meaning treated by law as if they had, disposed of their capital property at fair market value immediately before death. So every untaxed gain on land, shares and investments comes due in the final tax return, called the terminal return.

The problem for a developer is cash. The gain may sit mostly in private company shares and land that cannot be sold quickly. The estate owes tax but may have little cash to pay it. That can force a sale at a bad time, which is the developer's trap from an earlier lesson, arriving at the worst possible moment.

Registered plans have their own rules. In general, the value of an RRSP or RRIF is included in income at death unless it passes in a way the law allows to roll over, such as to a spouse [unverified — confirm independently].

The framework

These are concepts. Each one needs professional design before it is used.

  1. Measure the exposure. List each capital asset, its tax cost and today's value. The difference is the gain that death would trigger.
  2. Defer to a spouse. Section 70(6) of the Income Tax Act (Canada) generally allows property left to a spouse or common-law partner, or to a qualifying spousal trust, to pass at its tax cost, so the gain is deferred until the spouse disposes of it or dies.
  3. Cap the growth with a freeze. An estate freeze, from an earlier lesson, fixes the value of your shares today so future growth belongs to the next generation. The tax at your death is limited to the frozen value.
  4. Fund the tax. Life insurance owned by the right party can provide cash at death to pay the tax without a forced sale.
  5. Use the estate's tax position. An estate can qualify as a graduated rate estate for a limited period, defined in section 248(1) of the Income Tax Act (Canada), which can give some tax advantages [unverified — confirm independently].
  6. Watch for double tax on private shares. Without planning, the same growth in a private company can be taxed once at death and again when the company pays out its assets. Advisers use post-death planning to reduce this [unverified — confirm independently].

A worked example

This example is hypothetical. All numbers are round and invented for teaching. No tax rate is stated.

A developer's holding company shares have a tax cost of 500,000 and are worth 4,500,000. He also owns a rental property with a tax cost of 600,000, now worth 1,000,000. If he died today and left everything to his children, the deemed gains would be 4,000,000 on the shares and 400,000 on the rental. The estate holds only 150,000 in cash.

Plan A: leave everything to his spouse, or to a spousal trust that meets the rules. The gains are deferred until the spouse's death. This buys time but does not remove the tax.

Plan B: an estate freeze now at 4,500,000, so future growth goes to his children through a family trust. The gain at his death is capped at today's 4,000,000 rather than growing further.

Plan C: a life insurance policy sized by his accountant to the expected tax at the second death, so the estate is not forced to sell land.

Most real plans combine all three.

Professional Sign-Off Required: tax lawyer and chartered professional accountant (CPA); licensed insurance adviser for the policy.

The beginner mistake

The beginner mistake is to think "my spouse gets everything, so there is no tax." The spousal rollover defers the tax. It does not cancel it. The full bill comes at the second death, often larger because values kept growing.

The second mistake is to give property to children while alive to "avoid tax at death." A gift to an adult child is usually itself a disposition at fair market value [unverified — confirm independently], so the tax arrives sooner, not later.

How you will use it

Build a death tax table: asset, tax cost, value, gain, and who receives it. Ask your accountant to estimate the tax at your death and at your spouse's death, and to show how much cash the estate would have. The gap between tax and cash is your planning target. Revisit the table every two years and after any freeze, sale or large purchase, because the numbers move every time values change.
checklist: List each capital asset with its tax cost and today's value.
Calculate the gain that death would trigger on each.
Ask whether a spousal rollover or spousal trust fits your plan.
Consider whether an estate freeze would cap future growth.
Compare the expected tax at death with the cash the estate would have.
Ask about insurance sized to the gap.
Ask your CPA about post-death planning for private company shares.

selftest.q: A developer says, "I am leaving everything to my wife, so death tax is not my problem." What is wrong with that view?
selftest.a: Leaving property to a spouse or qualifying spousal trust generally defers the deemed disposition under section 70(6), but does not remove it. At the spouse's death the full gain, often larger by then, is taxed under section 70(5). He should measure the gain at both deaths, consider a freeze to cap growth, and consider insurance to pay the tax. A tax lawyer and CPA must sign off.

apply: Write a table of your three largest assets with tax cost, value and the gain that death would trigger today.
sources: Income Tax Act (Canada): section 70(5) (deemed disposition at death), section 70(6) (transfer to spouse or spousal trust) and the definition of graduated rate estate in section 248(1), cited by name; confirm current text with a CPA. RRSP and RRIF treatment at death, graduated rate estate benefits, double tax on private shares, post-death planning, and the treatment of gifts to adult children are tagged [unverified — confirm independently]. No tax rate or inclusion rate is stated. Figures hypothetical. Education only; not tax advice.
signoff: Professional Sign-Off Required: tax lawyer and chartered professional accountant (CPA); licensed insurance adviser.

title: Beneficiary designations, joint ownership and probate traps
summary: Many assets pass at death without going through your will, either because you named a beneficiary on the account or because you own the asset jointly. These shortcuts can save probate time and cost, but they can also contradict your will, leave the tax with the wrong person, and start family disputes.
body:
Bottom line. Your will does not control everything you own. Named beneficiaries and joint owners can take assets directly, outside the will. That can be fast and cheap, or it can quietly undo the plan in your will. Line them up on purpose.

In plain English

Probate is the court process that confirms a will is valid and confirms the executor's authority. Banks, land titles offices and others often need a probate grant before they will deal with the executor. Probate takes time and has fees, which vary by province [unverified — confirm independently].

Two common ways to pass assets without probate:

  • Beneficiary designations. On many registered accounts, such as an RRSP, a RRIF or a TFSA, and on life insurance, you can name who receives the money at death. The money usually goes straight to that person, not to the estate [unverified — confirm independently].
  • Joint ownership with right of survivorship. If you own land or a bank account as joint tenants, when one owner dies the other usually becomes sole owner automatically.

Both are useful. Both are also easy to set up and forget. And both act on their own, whatever your will says.

The framework

  1. List every asset that can pass outside the will. Registered accounts, insurance policies, pensions, and anything held jointly.
  2. Check each designation and each title. Who is named today? Many designations were filled in years ago and never updated.
  3. Compare with the will. Add up what each person receives in total, inside and outside the will. Unequal results are common and often accidental.
  4. Check who pays the tax. In general, the tax on a registered plan at death can fall on the estate even when the money goes directly to a named beneficiary [unverified — confirm independently]. One child gets the money and the estate, meaning all the children, pays the tax.
  5. Check joint ownership carefully. In Canada, when a parent puts an asset into joint names with an adult child for no payment, the law presumes the child holds it in trust for the parent's estate unless the parent's intention was a gift. The Supreme Court of Canada set this out in Pecore v. Pecore, 2007 SCC 17. So the "automatic" result is often disputed.
  6. Weigh the other risks of joint ownership. A joint owner's creditors or separating spouse may claim against the asset, and you may need the joint owner's signature to sell or refinance.

A worked example

This example is hypothetical. All numbers are round and invented for teaching.

A widowed developer has three children. His will divides his estate equally. His assets: a RRIF worth 600,000 naming his eldest child as beneficiary, from a form signed twenty years ago; a rental condo worth 500,000 he put into joint names with his youngest child "to avoid probate"; and a holding company worth 1,500,000 that passes under the will.

At his death, the eldest receives the RRIF directly. The youngest claims the condo as surviving joint owner. The will divides only the company shares. And the tax on the RRIF is charged to the estate, reducing what all three share.

The middle child disputes the condo, citing the presumption from Pecore. The family goes to court. The probate saving is lost many times over in legal fees and a broken relationship.

A review would have named the estate, or all three children, on the RRIF, documented the intention for the condo in writing, and checked that the totals matched his wish of equal shares.

Professional Sign-Off Required: wills and estates lawyer; chartered professional accountant (CPA).

The beginner mistake

The beginner mistake is to add a child to a title or account "to avoid probate" without writing down whether it is a gift or a convenience, and without telling the other children. That single missing sentence is often the whole dispute.

The second mistake is to change the will and forget the designations. A new will does not usually change a beneficiary named on an account [unverified — confirm independently].

How you will use it

Once a year, print every designation and every joint title and put them beside your will. Make a totals table: each person, what they receive inside the will, what they receive outside it, and who bears the tax. If the totals are not what you intend, fix the designation or the title first, because that is quicker and cheaper than a new will. Keep a signed note of your intention for every joint asset with a child. Ask your lawyer whether any probate saving is worth the control and dispute risk you give up.

For company shares, remember that a beneficiary designation is usually not available, so they usually pass under the will or the shareholder agreement. That is why the totals table matters: the shares are often the largest asset, and the shortcuts on smaller assets can tip the balance between your children without anyone intending it.
checklist: List every registered account, insurance policy and pension with its named beneficiary.
List every asset held jointly and how it is held.
Compare totals inside and outside the will for each person.
Ask who bears the tax on each registered plan at death.
Write down your intention for any joint asset with an adult child.
Update designations whenever you change your will.
Weigh any probate saving against loss of control and dispute risk.

selftest.q: You add your son to the title of a rental property as joint tenant so it passes without probate. Your will splits everything equally between your son and daughter. What can go wrong?
selftest.a: The property may pass to your son outside the will, making the split unequal. Under Pecore v. Pecore, 2007 SCC 17, a gratuitous transfer to an adult child is presumed held in trust for the estate unless you intended a gift, so your daughter may dispute it. The property is also exposed to your son's creditors or a separation, and you may need his signature to sell or refinance. Write down your intention and have a wills and estates lawyer review it.

apply: List every account and asset with a named beneficiary or a joint owner, and next to each write who receives it at your death.
sources: Pecore v. Pecore, 2007 SCC 17 (Supreme Court of Canada), cited by name for the presumption of resulting trust on gratuitous transfers to adult children; read the decision before relying on it. Probate fees, the effect of designations, who bears tax on registered plans at death, and whether a will can change a designation are tagged [unverified — confirm independently] and vary by province and plan. Figures hypothetical. Education only; not legal or tax advice.
signoff: Professional Sign-Off Required: wills and estates lawyer; chartered professional accountant (CPA).
